passage: The birthday party in the Andheri building ran right through Mohit's nap time. By five he was a different child. When his father, Deepak, handed him the blue cup instead of the red one, Mohit screamed and flung it. When a balloon popped, he dropped flat on the lobby floor, kicking. A neighbour frowned. 'So naughty!' Deepak only knelt, lifted him and carried him upstairs, drew the curtains and lay beside him. Mohit sobbed twice and was asleep within minutes.

qa.q: Which cup did Deepak hand Mohit?
qa.a: The blue cup instead of the red one.

qa.q: Why did Mohit scream over the cup?
qa.a: He was exhausted and overwhelmed after missing his nap, so a tiny frustration felt huge.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped?
qa.a: He did not scold; he carried Mohit to a dark, quiet room and lay beside him until he slept.

qa.q: How might the neighbour see Mohit's kicking?
qa.a: The neighbour sees naughtiness, not a tired toddler who has run out of ways to cope.

grounding: A toddler who missed his nap melts down over small things, and sleep, not discipline, is what he needs.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage:
Daycare note for Siddharth's parents
At four, Siddharth was racing laps round the room, shrieking with laughter and knocking over the block tower. It looked like fun, but he was rubbing his eyes between laps. My colleague wanted to put him in time-out. I thought he was overtired, not naughty. I dimmed the lights and sat with him on the mat with his soft rabbit. Two minutes later he burst into tears, then fell asleep on my lap. He had skipped his nap today.
Kiran

qa.q: What did Kiran notice Siddharth doing between laps?
qa.a: Rubbing his eyes.

qa.q: Why did Kiran decide against time-out?
qa.a: Kiran felt concerned that Siddharth was overtired, not naughty, and wanted him to rest rather than be punished.

qa.q: What did Kiran do instead?
qa.a: Dimmed the lights and sat with Siddharth on the mat with his soft rabbit until he could fall asleep.

qa.q: What was the wild running like for Siddharth?
qa.a: He was probably so tired he couldn't settle, so the laughter tipped into tears once the room calmed.

grounding: A carer reads a toddler's wild, loud play as a sign that a nap is overdue rather than misbehaviour.

passage:
Bedtime notes for Farida
Bedtime was a battle all last week: bargaining, crying, running off. This week I kept the same steps every night. Warm bath at seven, lamp turned low, the 'chanda mama' song twice, then one long cuddle and her toy elephant. No scolding, no extra stories. On Monday she cried for a while. By Thursday she was yawning in the bath and pointing to the lamp herself. Tonight she was asleep before the second song ended.
Harsha

qa.q: What song did Harsha sing?
qa.a: The 'chanda mama' song, twice.

qa.q: How did Farida seem to feel about bedtime by Thursday?
qa.a: She seemed calm and safe, yawning in the bath and pointing to the lamp because she knew what came next.

qa.q: Why did the same steps every night work better than bargaining?
qa.a: The predictable routine told Farida's body that sleep was safe, so she stopped fighting it.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha scolded or added extra stories?
qa.a: Farida would be left guessing and upset, and bedtime would likely stay a battle.

grounding: A carer uses a calm, repeated wind-down routine that helps a toddler feel safe going to sleep.

passage: The children's ward lights dimmed at eight. Arohi, in the bed by the window after a small operation on her ear, sat up at once. 'Papa, I need water.' Vikas gave her a sip. 'Papa, one more story.' He told a very short one about a sleepy owl. 'Papa, one more hug.' He hugged her. Then she whispered, 'What if you go home when I'm asleep?' So that was it. 'I'm sleeping right here in this chair all night,' Vikas said calmly, resting his hand on her blanket. Arohi held his finger, and her eyes closed.

qa.q: Where did Vikas say he would sleep?
qa.a: Right here in this chair all night.

qa.q: What was Arohi worried about behind all her requests?
qa.a: She was scared that Papa would go home while she was asleep in the dark ward.

qa.q: What worked to settle Arohi?
qa.a: Vikas gave short, calm answers and reassured her he would stay, with his hand on her blanket.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt as the requests kept coming?
qa.a: He may have felt tired or a little impatient at first, then tender once he understood she was afraid.

grounding: A young child's bedtime requests turn out to be a bid for reassurance, and calm, short answers settle her.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage:
'Saurabh, she's up again. Third time.'
'I heard. I have a meeting at nine.'
'And I don't have work? I've been up since two!'
From the next room Mishti wailed, 'Mamaaa!'
In the morning Binita snapped at Mishti over spilt milk, then cried in the bathroom. Saurabh found her there.
'I'm turning into a monster.'
'No. We're just not sleeping. I snapped at you last night too.'
'So what now?'
'Tonight you sleep in the other room with earplugs. I do the nights. Tomorrow we swap. And we ask your mother to take Mishti one afternoon so we can both nap.'

qa.q: Since when had Binita been awake?
qa.a: Since two.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she cried in the bathroom?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed after snapping at Mishti, afraid she was turning into a monster.

qa.q: What plan did Saurabh suggest?
qa.a: Taking turns with the nights, earplugs in the other room, and asking Binita's mother to take Mishti one afternoon so they can nap.

qa.q: How might Mishti experience her parents' snapping?
qa.a: Mishti may feel confused or upset at being scolded over spilt milk, not knowing her parents are simply exhausted.

grounding: Parents worn down by a child's night waking snap and feel guilty, and they plan real rest instead of relying on willpower.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Worst day. Last night the neighbours had a wedding band till late and I couldn't sleep. Today in class my eyes kept closing. Ma'am told us to do questions 1 to 5 on page 42, and I did 6 to 10. Varun laughed. I told him to shut up and then I started crying, in front of everyone! Ma'am said I was being careless. I wasn't. My head felt like cotton wool and I was trying SO hard.
At home Mummy saw my face and asked what happened. When I told her about the band, she said, 'You're not lazy, you're tired.' She wrote a note to Ma'am. Early bed tonight.
Mehak

qa.q: Which questions did Mehak do by mistake?
qa.a: Mehak did questions 6 to 10.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when Ma'am called the work careless?
qa.a: Mehak felt hurt and misunderstood, having tried hard with a foggy, sleepy head.

qa.q: How could Ma'am support a child like Mehak next time?
qa.a: Ma'am could gently ask whether Mehak had slept well, instead of calling the mistake careless.

qa.q: What might Mummy's note help Ma'am understand?
qa.a: It could show Ma'am that the mistakes came from a sleepless night, not laziness, so she can respond kindly.

grounding: A schoolchild short of sleep forgets instructions, turns teary and is called careless, though effort alone cannot fix the fog.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4A
Madhav is usually the one cracking jokes at the start of the day. This week he has been slumped on his desk, yawning, snapping at his partner and taking ages to open his notebook. My first thought on Tuesday was to send him to the headmistress for not working. I held back and asked him quietly at lunch how he was sleeping. He said his baby sister cries at night, the family shares one room, and he has been doing homework late. I have cut his homework this week and will speak to his mother on Friday about a quieter bedtime corner.
Harish

qa.q: Why has Madhav been sleeping badly?
qa.a: His baby sister cries at night, the family shares one room, and he has been doing homework late.

qa.q: What was Harish's first impulse on Tuesday, and what feeling was behind it?
qa.a: Harish felt frustrated and was tempted to send Madhav to the headmistress for not working.

qa.q: Why was the quiet question at lunch the better choice?
qa.a: It uncovered the real cause, lost sleep, so Harish could cut homework and plan with the family instead of punishing.

qa.q: What might it be like for Madhav to be asked kindly instead of punished?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and understood, since he was too tired to work, not lazy.

grounding: A teacher notices a cheerful child slumped and irritable and asks gently about sleep instead of punishing.

passage:

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Every morning last term began with me shouting at Aditi's door at six. 'Get up! You'll miss the van!' And every morning I got grunts, a slammed door and a girl who wouldn't look at me over breakfast. My neighbour laughed, 'Usha, your flat sounds like a war.' I thought my daughter had turned lazy and rude. Then, waiting at the dentist's, I read that teenagers' body clocks shift later, so they genuinely can't fall asleep early. I felt ashamed of all the shouting. That evening I asked Aditi what might help instead of ordering her. We agreed on phones charging in the hall by ten-thirty and the same wake-up time every day, even Sundays. I bought her a loud alarm clock and stopped being her alarm. Mornings are still slow, but we talk again.

qa.q: What time do the phones go to charge in the hall?
qa.a: By ten-thirty.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after reading about teenagers' body clocks?
qa.a: Usha felt ashamed of all the shouting, realising Aditi genuinely couldn't fall asleep early.

qa.q: What agreement did Usha and Aditi reach?
qa.a: Phones charging in the hall by ten-thirty, the same wake-up time daily, and a loud alarm clock instead of Usha's shouting.

qa.q: How might Aditi have experienced those shouting mornings?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt exhausted and attacked, which came out as grunts and slammed doors.

grounding: A parent who shouts at a sleepy teenager learns about body clocks and negotiates phone cut-offs and a steady wake time.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, board exam week
At 2 a.m. I found Rafiq at the common-room table with three textbooks open, a flask of tea and red eyes. He said he planned to stay up all night, because every hour awake meant more marks. The next afternoon, after his chemistry paper, he came to my office shaking. He had blanked on formulas he knew well and was panicking about physics the next day. We made a plan together: revise only his summary sheets until nine, lights out by eleven, breakfast before the exam. He grumbled but agreed. After physics he came by to say his mind had felt clear.
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Rafiq have with him at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Three textbooks open and a flask of tea.

qa.q: How was Rafiq feeling after his chemistry paper?
qa.a: He was shaken and panicking, having blanked on formulas he knew and dreading physics the next day.

qa.q: What calmer plan did Ujjwal and Rafiq make?
qa.a: Revise only summary sheets until nine, lights out by eleven, and breakfast before the exam.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have felt finding Rafiq awake at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Ujjwal was likely worried that losing sleep would weaken Rafiq's memory before the exams.

grounding: A student believes cramming all night means more learning, loses memory and calm, and a plan that protects sleep helps.
